newsitem.title: USA: Jury resumes deliberations in Oklahoma bomb case.
newsitem.headline: Jury resumes deliberations in Oklahoma bomb case.

text.p: Jury deliberations stretched into a third day on Sunday in the trial of accused Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh, as anxiety grew among waiting survivors and relatives of those killed in the devastating blast.

"I didn't think the jury would have taken this long. That's scary," said Jannie Coverdale, whose grandsons Elijah and Aaron were among the 168 bombing victims. "Somebody on the jury doesn't want to find him guilty."
The panel of seven men and five women has been sequestered since starting deliberations on Friday morning. They deliberated a full day on Friday and another full day on Saturday.

They are weighing murder and conspiracy charges against McVeigh, 29, a former soldier, who is accused of blowing up the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995. The explosion killed 168 people and wounded more than 500 others.
He faces the possibility of a death sentence or life in prison if convicted.
Attorneys in the case adopted a more cautionary tone as to what a third day of deliberations meant.
"I don't know if you can view a long or a short deliberation either way," said Christopher Tritico, a member of the McVeigh defence team as he walked into the Denver courthouse to see his client.
"There's no way to tell," he said.
Federal Judge Richard Matsch has allowed the jurors to set their own hours, making predictions of their schedule difficult.
Defence attorneys said McVeigh was reading and talking on the telephone to friends as he waited in a basement prison cell.
"He's holding up as well as I would expect him to at this juncture," Tritico said after his visit with McVeigh.
Survivors and family members waited on Sunday at a nearby church, doing crossword puzzles and watching television.

Sponsored by the Justice Department, groups of survivors and relatives have been attending the trial in week-long shifts, and on Sunday, many were preparing to return home to allow another 24-member group to come to Denver.
"I wish the verdict would have come in yesterday so the people that were up here could hear it," said Charles Tomlin, whose son Rick was killed in the explosion.
"They sure wanted to hear it," he said, adding, "Then again, if it was the wrong verdict, they wouldn't want to hear that."

Local defence attorney David Japha, who has followed the trial closely, said he read little or nothing into the length of the deliberations nor the fact that the jurors have not returned with questions or requests for testimony to be re-read.

"They're looking at each and every element. Did each and every element get proved up beyond a reasonable doubt?" he said. "And if you look at that, they're not really spending an inordinate amount of time."
As the jury deliberated, hundreds of journalists also kept watch at the federal courthouse in Denver, where the testimony in the trial began on April 24.
